procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 28.06.2017 of the High Court of Karnataka at Bengaluru in Criminal Appeal No. 531 of 2011 C/w Criminal Appeal No. 248 of 2011.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Karnataka at Bangalore passed a judgment on 28.06.2017 in Criminal Appeal No. 531 of 2011 c/w Criminal Appeal No. 248 of 2011.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Accused no. 1 in a crime registered at Chamarajanagar Rural Police Station, Karnataka, appealed to the Supreme Court, aggrieved by the conviction and sentence imposed by the District & Sessions Judge, Chamarajanagar in Sessions Case No. 59 of 2009 (dated 17th January 2011) and the subsequent judgment of the High Court in Criminal Appeal No.531 of 2011 c/w Criminal Appeal No.248 of 2011 passed on 28.06.2017.

directions: The bail bonds, if any, furnished by the appellant-accused stand discharged.
The appellant-accused is entitled for refund of the fine amount deposited by him.

issue.issue_text: Whether the conviction and sentence imposed on the appellant-accused for the offence under Section 436 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code are sustainable in law, considering the evidence on record.

facts: The appellant (accused no. 1) was convicted by the Trial Court for setting fire to a thatched shed (offence under Section 436 IPC) along with three other co-accused.
The High Court acquitted accused nos. 2 to 4 but upheld the conviction of accused no. 1 and enhanced his sentence to six months imprisonment and a fine.
There were pre-existing civil disputes and prior complaints between the appellant and the family of the main witness (PW-1).
The prosecution's case relied on the testimony of witnesses PW-1, PW-2, and PW-3, who were all interested parties due to the family relationship and ongoing disputes.
Additional documentary evidence was filed by the defense before the High Court but was not considered.
law: A criminal conviction requires the prosecution to prove the guilt of the accused beyond a reasonable doubt.
The testimony of interested witnesses must be scrutinized with caution, especially in the absence of corroboration from independent witnesses.
Material contradictions in the prosecution's evidence can render the testimony unreliable and weaken the case against the accused.
application: The Supreme Court found that the lower courts had committed a serious error by overlooking several material contradictions in the prosecution's evidence.
**Contradiction regarding witnesses:** PW-1 and PW-2 did not mention the presence of PW-3 at the scene, whereas PW-3 claimed to have been present.

**Contradiction regarding damages:** PW-1 and PW-2 testified that books and clothes were burnt, which was contrary to the official mahazar (investigation report) that only mentioned the partial burning of a fan and the roof.

**Contradiction regarding occupancy:** PW-7 (the police officer) admitted that nobody was living in the shed, directly contradicting the testimony of PW-2 and PW-3 who claimed PW-1's family was staying there.
The Court noted that the only direct witnesses (PWs 1-3) were interested parties due to the existing property disputes, which created a possibility of false implication.
No independent witnesses were examined by the prosecution to corroborate the testimony of these interested witnesses.
The Court also pointed out that the High Court failed to consider the additional documentary evidence filed by the defense.
These contradictions and the reliance on uncorroborated, interested testimony were deemed by the Supreme Court to have resulted in "perverse findings" by the lower courts.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that due to the material contradictions in the evidence and the lack of independent witnesses, the prosecution had failed to prove the appellant's guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. The Court held that allowing the conviction to stand would result in a miscarriage of justice and, therefore, set aside the judgments of the High Court and the trial court, acquitting the appellant.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the conviction and sentence imposed on the appellant-accused for the offence under Section 436 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code are sustainable in law, considering the evidence on record.
appellant_arguments: The conviction was erroneously recorded as there was no acceptable evidence on record.
The prosecution's case relied solely on the interested testimony of witnesses PWs-1 to 3, with no independent eyewitnesses examined.
There were material contradictions in the oral evidence of witnesses PWs-1 to 5, which were not properly considered by the trial court or the High Court.
Additional documentary evidence filed by the appellant before the appellate court under Section 391 of the Cr.P.C. was not considered by the High Court.
The State failed to prove the guilt of the accused beyond a reasonable doubt.
respondent_arguments: The oral evidence of witnesses PWs-1 to 5 is consistent and sufficient to record a conviction.
The accused intentionally set fire to the dwelling house due to property disputes among the brothers.
The trial court and the High Court rightly recorded the conviction based on the evidence.
The initial sentence of only a fine was contrary to Section 436 IPC, and the High Court correctly enhanced it to imprisonment and a fine.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A conviction is liable to be set aside if an appellate court, upon review of the evidence and material on record, finds that allowing the judgment to stand would lead to a miscarriage of justice.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The trial court and the appellate court committed a serious error in convicting the accused, as the conviction was based on perverse findings. The lower courts failed to notice material contradictions in the prosecution's oral evidence, improperly relied on the interested testimony of witnesses PWs-1 to 3 without any independent corroboration, and completely failed to consider additional documentary evidence filed by the appellant.
legal_tests_applied: Assessment of whether lower court findings are 'perverse' due to a failure to properly consider material contradictions in evidence.
Evaluation of whether a conviction based solely on the 'interested testimony' of witnesses, without any 'independent person... examined as a direct witness to the incident,' is sustainable.
The overarching principle that a conviction must be set aside if allowing it to stand 'will lead to miscarriage of justice'.
policy_considerations: The Court determined that if the impugned judgments were allowed to stand, it would 'lead to a miscarriage of justice,' thus necessitating that they be set aside.
